    </trailer>
</message>

Thus, the expanded printout can be used not only for human-readable output, but also as a machine-readable alternative representation of the MT message, which can be used in various scenarios.

Tip

Notice this XML format is more feature rich than the MT-XML format available in the open source library Prowide Core because it includes the full message structure, including sequences and fields, as well as labels and descriptions.

docs.title: Printout XML Schema
docs.text:
The expanded printout in XML format can be validated using an automatically generated XML Schema Definition (XSD). This XSD reflects the internal scheme model of each MT type and ensures structural correctness of the printed output.

The utility class PrintoutSchemaGen can be used to programmatically generate the XSD content for a given MT type:

String xsd = PrintoutSchemaGen.generateSchema(MtType.MT103);

Once the schema content is generated, the printed XML can be validated against it using standard XML tools:

SwiftMessage mt103 = SwiftMessage.parse("{1:F01...}{2:I103...}{4:\n:20:...\n...-}");

String xml = new PrintoutWriter(Locale.ENNGLISH, new XmlPrintoutVisitor()).print(mt103);

SchemaFactory factory = SchemaFactory.newInstance(XMLConstants.W3C_XML_SCHEMA_NS_URI);
Schema schema = factory.newSchema(new StreamSource(new StringReader(xsd)));

Validator validator = schema.newValidator();
validator.validate(new StreamSource(new StringReader(xml)));

This validation ensures that:

  • Required and optional fields follow the correct order and cardinality
  • Field repetitions and letter options match the SWIFT specification
  • Sequences and nested structures are printed consistently with the internal model

Info

The schema is generated dynamically because the structure of each MT type varies significantly. Notice these XML formats are tied to the internal model of each MT. Conversely, the MT-XML format from the open source library Prowide Core is a generic representation for each combination of fields, thus for any MT, even invalid MTs.

docs.title: Printout XML to MT
docs.text:
Round-tripping the printout XML back into MT objects and canonical XML

It may happen that the expanded printout is not the final step but an intermediate representation that must later be consumed by other systems. For these use-cases the library provides a small utility set that lets you Convert the printout XML back into a SwiftMessage model.

The following helpers are located in com.prowidesoftware.swift.io.printout:

Helper Purpose Typical next step XmlPrintout2SwiftMessageTransformer Parses the printout XML directly into a SwiftMessage (the same class you obtain when reading the original FIN) Continue working with the Prowide object model (e.g. validation, translation, network copy, etc.) XmlPrintout2MtXmlTransformer Transforms the printout XML into the canonical MT-XML from Prowide Core, that can be consumed by the XMLParser Feed to any XML pipeline, compare with other canonical messages, or parse back with XMLParser

The transformer detects whether the MT type uses sequence delimiters based on field 15a or 16R/16S and rebuilds them accordingly. For all other MTs the fields are copied verbatim.

docs.title: End-to-end example
docs.text:
String originalFin = "{1:F01AAAAUS33AXXX0000000000}{2:I103BBBBUS33XXXXU2}{3:{108:FOOB3926BE868XXX}}{4:"
        + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + ":20:11111111" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + ":23B:CRED" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + ":32A:250718EUR1234567,89" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + ":33B:USD89431,40" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + ":50A:/12345678901234567890" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + "AAAAUS33XXX" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + ":59:/12345678901234567890" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + "JOE DOE" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + "MyStreet 1234" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + ":71A:OUR" + FINWriterVisitor.SWIFT_EOL
        + "-}";
AbstractMT mt = AbstractMT.parse(originalFin);
String printoutXml = new PrintoutWriter(Locale.ENGLISH, new XmlPrintoutVisitor()).print(mt);
SwiftMessage model = new XmlPrintoutToSwiftMessageTransformer().apply(printoutXml);
String finalFin = model.message();

In the above example the original FIN message and the final FIN message are the same. This is just to illustrate the round-trip process. On a real scenario the intermediate XML would be used for data exchange, enrichment or other purposes.

Warning

Some of the MT header fields are set to its default value: Logical Terminal identifier, Session Number and Sequence Number. This is because the printout XML does not propagate this information. Anyway, these fields are normally initialized by the SWIFT interface when the message is released or received.

With these utilities you can seamlessly move from FIN → printout XML → object model or FIN → printout XML → canonical XML making the expanded printout in XML a genuinely two-way representation of the message data.

docs.title: MT messages structure schemes in XML
docs.text:
Message schemes are a central and powerful part of the component. Message structure schemes are mainly used by the message validator module, but they may be suitable for multiple purposes in a SWIFT message management application. For example, they can be the base information source of a message creation user interface.

The schemes are defined by means of an XML, and provided as a Java model in the library. The structure is statically defined in a SchemeNNN class.

The following examples serve to quickly understand the content and general structure of these XML schemas:

Example 1: Simple message with two inner sequences.

<?xml version = "1.0" encoding = "UTF-8"?>
<scheme name="203" release = "2011">
    <sequence minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1">
        <sequence minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" name="A">
            <field id="19" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1"/>
            <field id="30" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1"/>
            <field id="52" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, D"/>
            <field id="53" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, B, D"/>
            <field id="54" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, B, D"/>
            <field id="72" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1"/>
        </sequence>
        <sequence minRepetitions="2" maxRepetitions="10" name="B" description="Returned Transaction">
            <field id="20" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1"/>
            <field id="21" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1"/>
            <field id="32" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="B"/>
            <field id="56" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, D"/>
            <field id="57" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, B, D"/>
            <field id="58" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, D"/>
            <field id="72" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1"/>
        </sequence>
    </sequence>
</scheme>

Example 2: with two level sequences.

<?xml version = "1.0" encoding = "UTF-8"?>
<scheme name="541" description="Receive Against Payment Instruction">
    <sequence minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1">
        <sequence name="A" description="General Information" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1">
            <field id="16" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="R" qualifiers="GENL"/>
            <field id="20" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="C" qualifiers="SEME"/>
            <field id="23" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="G"/>
            <field id="98" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, C, E" qualifiers="PREP"/>
            <field id="99" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="4" letterOptions="B"/>
            <sequence name="A1" description="Linkages" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="UNLIMITED">
                <field id="16" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="R" qualifiers="LINK"/>
                <field id="22" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="F" qualifiers="LINK"/>
                <field id="13" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="A, B" qualifiers="LINK"/>
                <field id="20" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="C"/>
                <field id="36" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="B" qualifiers="PAIR"/>
                <field id="16" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="S" qualifiers="LINK"/>
            </sequence>
            <field id="16" minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="S" qualifiers="GENL"/>
        </sequence>
        (...)
    </sequence>
</scheme>

docs.title: Loading schemes
docs.text:
To access the out-of-the-box schemes, the MtType enumeration can be used. This enumeration is updated yearly and contains all types available for the current SRU.

For example, MtType.MT103.scheme() will return a Scheme object with the specific message schema for MT103.

docs.title: Semantics of XML elements and attributes
docs.text:
• scheme: Mandatory container tag and root element of every scheme. It identifies the MT being structured. Attributes:

    • name: mandatory identifier of the scheme, usually related to an MT name, as mentioned in the SWIFT Handbook.
    • description: Optional description of message scheme.

  • sequence: All message fields must be part of a specific sequence. At least one main sequence is required, even if the standard does not mention it. Sequences can be nested, conforming to the blocks and subblocks of the message as needed. Attributes:

    • name: Optional name for the sequence, can be a letter based name as used through the SWIFT handbook or any functional name related to the contents of the sequence.
    • minRepetitions: Mandatory attribute accepting an integer number to indicate the minimum repetitions expected of the sequence. A value of "0" means that the sequence will be optional, a value of "1" means that the sequence is mandatory, and a value of "n" (being n an integer number greater than 1) means that the sequence is mandatory and at least n sequences must be filled for a message to be valid according to this scheme definition.
    • maxRepetitions: Mandatory attribute accepting a positive integer number greater or equal to 1 to indicate the maximum allowed repetitions of the sequence. A value of "1" means that the sequence can have up to one repetition and a value of "n" (being n an integer number greater than 1) means that the sequence is mandatory and at most n sequences can be filled for a message to be valid according to this scheme definition. To allow an unlimited number of repetitions, the literal "UNLIMITED" can be used.

  • field: This element defines a SWIFT field. Represents a set of zero or more fields of the sequence. Repetition attributes must be present, as well as "id". The letterOption attribute is optional, and the literal "NONE" is supported. A letter option indicating "A, B, NONE" on a field with id "50" for example, means that the field can be 50A, 50B or 50 with no letter option. It accepts the same tag attributes as the sequence element, plus:

    • id: Mandatory attribute to indicate the field numeric identifier without the letter options.
    • letterOptions: Optional attribute to indicate the letter options admitted for the field. The letter option must be ppercase, and it admits a single letter or a comma separated list of letters. The literal "NONE" can also be used to indicate that the field admits an empty letter option (Notice that a "NONE" value is the default for the element, meaning that if the letterOption attribute is not present, the field will not accept letter options. The literal is useful for particular fields where it is valid to a letter option "A" for example as well as no letter option at all).
    • qualifiers: Optional attribute to specify fixed values for the field. The attribute value supports complex combination from a simple fixed literal to a combination of qualifiers per letter option and field’s components. For example, a simple value of "GENL" means that the field is expected to have the literal GENL as value. Multiple values can be indicated with a comma/whitespace separated list, for example: "SECU, SEGU, OTHR" meaning that the field can have any of the mentioned literals. If the field supports several letter options, the literal qualifiers can be indicated for particular letter options for example: "SECU, A.SEGU, B.OTHR" means that literal SEGU is expected for any letter option, SEGU is expected for letter option A, and OTHR for letter option B. By default the qualifier is validated against the first component of the field. If a specific field’s component is expected to have the qualifier, a letter, and component number combination can be expressed. For example, the qualifier J.5.ACCU means that for letter option J, field’s component 5 is expected to have the literal ACCU as value.

docs.title: Fieldsets
docs.text:
This section describes some advanced features of the XML schemes that may be useful to tune up validations on specific scenarios.

All messages for category 5, as well as some messages for category 3 have an extensive structure definition. These definitions are performed with the same XML described above, but including two special features: fieldsets and evaluations.

A fieldset is a definition of a message field that has several consecutive and unordered instances. All fields in the fieldset share the field number, but may accept different letter options and different qualifiers. For example, the following definition will accept up to three instances of field 20C with the qualifiers CORP, SEME and COAF, with two of them mandatory and one optional:

<fieldset id="20" letterOptions="C">
    <item minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" qualifiers="CORP"/>
    <item minRepetitions="1" maxRepetitions="1" qualifiers="SEME"/>
    <item minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" qualifiers="COAF"/>
</fieldset>

The validation of this structure is well covered by the SWIFT Handbook. Please notice that a fieldset is different from a field with repetitions because it can have different qualifiers, letter options, and expected repetitions of each item. It also is different from a sequence because the items can appear in the message in any order.

Semantic of the fieldset XML definition and attributes:

  • fieldset: Mandatory container tag and root element of every fieldset.Attributes:

    • id: Mandatory identifier field's number defined by the fieldset. All inner items will share this field number.
    • letterOption: Optional identification of the letter option. If this attribute is defined on the fieldset tag, all inner items will share the same expected letter options.
    • minRepetitions: Optional attribute accepting an integer number to indicate the minimum repetitions expected of all inner items of this fieldset. If this attribute is defined on the fieldset tag, all inner items will share the same expected minimum repetition.
    • maxRepetitions: Optional attribute accepting a positive integer number greater or equal to 1 to indicate the maximum allowed repetitions of all inner items of this fieldset. If this attribute is defined on the fieldset tag, all inner items will share the same expected maximum repetition.

  • item: Definition of each possible field instance into the container fieldset.Attributes:

    • letterOption: Optional identification of the letter option. This value can be overwritten if the letter option is defined at the container fieldset.
    • minRepetitions: Definition of the minimum repetitions expected for the field instance. This value can be overwritten if the letter option is defined at the container fieldset. If the attribute is not defined for the fieldset, it is mandatory to define it in the item.
    • maxRepetitions: Definition of the maximum repetitions expected for the field instance. This value can be overwritten if the letter option is defined at the container fieldset. If the attribute is not defined for the fieldset, it is mandatory to define it in the item.
    • qualifiers: Optional attribute to specify fixed values for the field.

docs.title: Qualifier validation evaluations
docs.text:
Qualifier validation elements are used to indicate the allowed field qualifiers and conditional qualifiers within field, fieldset and item elements.

Notice for simple cases where the field or item expects certain qualifiers, the direct qualifiers attribute described above suffices. However, for some message types the logic to determine the expected qualifier is more complex and has to be defined conditionally.

The qualifierValidation element might contain several attributes. Some attributes are used as a conditional, to determine if the actual validation applies. Plus the attributes to define the actual constraint. For example, the following definition will match fields 94B, with qualifiers PRIC or RATS, and if the DSS (data source definition) of the field is not set, then the conditional qualifier (component 3) must be LMAR, FIND, THEO or VEND.

<fieldset id="94" minRepetitions="0" maxRepetitions="1" letterOptions="B">
    <qualifierValidation notDssCondition="true" conditionalqualifiers="LMAR, FUND, THEO, VEND"/>
    <item qualifiers="PRIC"/>
    <item qualifiers="RATS"/>
</fieldset>

In the above example, the notDssCondition is the conditional and the conditionalQualifiers is the actual constraint.

The available attributes for the conditional part are:

  • notDssCondition: boolean value, when true, means the field’s DSS (data source definition) should not be present for the qualifier validation to apply.
  • letterCondition: string value with the field instance letter option (admits a csv list), the qualifier validation will be applied only if the field matches the letter.
  • qualifierCondition: a specific qualifier that the field must match in order for the conditional qualifier validation to apply.

The available attributes for the constraint are:

  • qualifiers(list): function that evaluates to true if the field main qualifier has any of the given values. The list parameter is a string value with one or many qualifiers, separated with a comma. Each qualifier may be prefixed with an integer to specify the component that will be checked (by default, the component checked is the component 1).
  • conditionalQualifiers(list): function that evaluates to true if the field conditional qualifier has any of the given values. The component used as a "conditional qualifier" is the third component. For example, when the field defines a data source scheme as the second component (for example 22F), or the second component if the field does not define a data source scheme (for example 12C). The conditional qualifier function is intended only for generic fields (Field that implements the interface GenericField). For all other fields, the verifyQualifier function should be used.

Then when defining the actual qualifiers or conditional qualifiers list in the constraint, a couple of fixed literal expressions are supported. These are needed just for two particular cases. These expressions are interpreted as literals, thus these specific strings are the only ones supported:

  • [3!n_NOT_ZERO]: string value that can be used in a qualifier list parameter and will evaluate to true if the component value is composed of three numbers and not 000.
  • [4!n_NOT_ZERO]: string value that can be used in a qualifier list parameter and will evaluate to true if the component value is composed of four numbers and not 000.

Several examples of qualifierValidation can be found in the included XML schemes of the package. For example:

<qualifierValidation letterCondition="C" conditionalqualifiers="GENR"/>
<qualifierValidation letterCondition="B" notDssCondition="true" conditionalqualifiers="AMOR, FAMT, UNIT"/>
<qualifierValidation letterCondition="C" qualifiers="3.AMOR, 3.FAMT, 3.UNIT"/>
<qualifierValidation qualifierCondition = "REST" notDssCondition="true" conditionalqualifiers="ACCT, ACCP, SUBR, REJT"/>
<qualifierValidation conditionalqualifiers="UNS, [3!n_NOT_ZERO]"/>

During the validation, the attributes in the qualifierValidation element are evaluated in order to determine if the input is valid or not. The validation engine will match the field/item only if all the attributes are evaluated as true. If an evaluation is false, the field may be reported as an unexpected field.

docs.title: XmlNode
docs.text: The XmlNode is a light-weight utility for managing XML structures with a DOM representation. It can be used as an alternative to the standard Java DOM API for light-way, fast and simple XML processing tasks.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
1. Tree Structure: Represents XML nodes as a tree with parent-child relationships.
  2. Attributes Management: Supports adding, updating, and retrieving attributes for nodes.
  3. Value Storage: Allows storing and retrieving textual content for nodes.
  4. Integration: Works seamlessly with the XmlParser for creating node trees from XML strings, files, or streams.
  5. Traversal: Supports traversal of the XML structure, including navigation to parent and child nodes.
  6. Path Navigation: Enables advanced navigation and filtering using path expressions and predicates.
  7. Cloning Support: Provides functionality to create deep copies of nodes, including their attributes and children, while avoiding circular dependencies.
  8. Deletion of Nodes: Supports deletion of nodes and their subtrees by specifying a path, ensuring clean-up of unwanted XML structures.
  9. Serialization: Supports serializing the XML node tree into properly formatted XML strings for storage or transmission.
  10. Dynamic Node Creation: Allows creating nodes dynamically along a specified path, including missing intermediate nodes, using the create() method.
  11. Error Handling: Gracefully handles parsing errors, invalid paths, and other exceptions, ensuring robust XML manipulation.

Limitations

1. The XmlNode is not namespace-aware.
2. The Xpath-like path navigation is limited to simple expressions.
3. Does not support comments, processing instructions or CDATA sections.

docs.title: Parsing XML Content (unmarshalling)
docs.text:
You can use the XmlParser to create a tree structure from XML:

String xmlContent = "<root><child>Value</child></root>";
XmlNode rootNode = XmlParser.parse(xmlContent);

The resulting XmlNode instance represents the root of the XML tree, and you can navigate through its children and attributes. Parsed content can also be modified and nodes can be added or removed.

Supported Input Formats for the parser:

  • String: Parse directly from an XML string.
  • File: Use XmlParser.parse(File file) to load XML from a file.
  • InputStream: Parse from an input stream for dynamic content.

The behavior for preserving or normalizing whitespace can be controlled through XmlParserConfiguration:

XmlParserConfiguration config = new XmlParserConfiguration();
config.preserveLineBreaks = false;
config.preserveWhitespaces = false;
XmlNode rootNode = XmlParser.parse(xmlContent, config);

docs.title: Serializing the XML (marshalling)
docs.text:
For serialization, the XmlNode class provides the xml() method to convert the node tree back into an XML string.

XmlNode root = XmlParser.parse("<root><child>ChildValue</child><child>AnotherValue</child></root>");
System.out.println(root.xml());

Sample Output: 

<root>
    <child>ChildValue</child>
    <child>AnotherValue</child>
</root>

Then a simple content-only printing is also available. The print method to output the structure in a human-friendly view, with indentation for hierarchy:

XmlNode root = XmlParser.parse("<root><child/><child><grandchild/></child><child><grandchild><greatgrandchild/></grandchild></child></root>");
root.print();

Sample Output: 

    root
        child
        child
            grandchild        
        child
            grandchild
                greatgrandchild

This is helpful for debugging and understanding the structure of the XML tree.

docs.title: Creating XML Content
docs.text:
The XML tree structure can also be created manually using the XmlNode class.

In this example we create a root element, and we add a child element to it:

XmlNode root = new XmlNode("root");
XmlNode child = root.addChild("child");
child.setValue("This is a child node.");

You can also dynamically create a node and assign a value in a single step:

XmlNode newNode = root.create("parent/child/grandchild", "Grandchild Value");
System.out.println(newNode.getValue()); // Outputs: Grandchild Value
  • Each XmlNode instance can store the element local name, a value (if it is a leaf node), and attributes.
  • Nodes maintain references to their parent and child nodes.
  • Values can be set and retrieved using setValue and getValue accessors.
node.setValue("Hello, world!");
String value = node.getValue();
System.out.println("Node Value: " + value);

Since the structure of the whole tree is loaded into memory, direct content manipulation is possible. You can find and update the node text content in the returned node instance. Any changes will be reflected in the tree when serialized into XML.

docs.title: Node Attributes
docs.text:
Attributes are key-value pairs associated with an XmlNode, often used to represent XML element attributes.

A specific model is provided for the attributes, which is XmlNodeAttribute and attributes are set as follows:

XmlNode node = new XmlNode("example");
node.addAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("id", "123"));
node.addAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("class", "test"));
  • Attributes are stored as a list of XmlNodeAttribute objects.
  • The XmlNodeAttribute class supports name-value pairs and provides methods for serialization into XML format.

Existing attributes can be retrieve attributes using the getAttributes method. Iterating through the list allows access to attribute names and values:

List<XmlNodeAttribute> attributes = node.getAttributes();
for (XmlNodeAttribute attr : attributes) {
    System.out.println(attr.getName() + "=" + attr.getValue());
}

Existing attributes can also be updated or removed, the same as with child nodes

You can check if a node has a specific attribute using the hasAttribute(XmlNodeAttribute attr) method.

Example:

XmlNode node = new XmlNode("example");
node.addAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("id", "123"));

boolean hasId = node.hasAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("id", "123"));
System.out.println(hasId); // Outputs: true

docs.title: Traversing the Node Tree
docs.text: The XmlNode tree structure allows intuitive navigation through parent and child relationships.

docs.title: Accessing Child Nodes
docs.text:
Use getChildren to retrieve all child nodes:

List<XmlNode> children = root.getChildren();
for (XmlNode child : children) {
    System.out.println(child.getName());
}
  • The getChildren method returns a list of child nodes.
  • A node can have multiple children, forming a tree structure.

docs.title: Navigating to the Parent Node
docs.text:
XmlNode parent = child.getParent();
System.out.println("Parent: " + parent.getName());

docs.title: Accessing Nodes by Path
docs.text:
The XmlNode class integrates with XPath-like navigation for filtering and advanced traversal.

Use getNodeByPath to locate nodes using XPath-like expressions:

XmlNode target = root.getNodeByPath("child/grandchild");
System.out.println(target.getName());

Supported Path Features:

  • Absolute Paths: /root/child
  • Relative Paths: ../sibling
  • Inner Paths: //sibling/grandchild
  • Advanced Predicates: child[@id='123']

docs.title: Using Predicates in Paths
docs.text:
Predicates allow filtering nodes by specific conditions. For example:

XmlNode filteredNode = root.getNodeByPath("child[@id='123']");

docs.title: Relative Paths
docs.text:
The XmlNode class supports relative paths for navigation:

XmlNode target = child.getNodeByPath("../sibling");
System.out.println(target.getName());

Examples:

  • ../ moves up one level.
  • ../../node moves up two levels and selects node tag.
  • //node/subnode will traverse all the entire tree and return the first node that contains a subnode as a child.

docs.title: Sibling Navigation
docs.text:
In addition to parent and child navigation, the XmlNode class supports accessing sibling nodes.

Example:

XmlNode root = XmlParser.parse("<root><sibling1/><sibling2/></root>");
XmlNode sibling1 = root.getChildren().get(0);
List<XmlNode> siblings = sibling1.siblings(null);

for (XmlNode sibling : siblings) {
    System.out.println(sibling.getName()); // Outputs: sibling2
}

docs.title: Recursive Navigation
docs.text:
The tree can be traversed recursively for complex operations:

void traverse(XmlNode node) {
    System.out.println(node.getName());
    if (node.hasChildren()) {
        for (XmlNode child : node.getChildren()) {
            traverse(child);
        }
    }
}
traverse(root);

docs.title: Recursive Value Retrieval
docs.text:
In addition to getValue(), the XmlNode class supports retrieving values recursively from child nodes.

Example:

XmlNode root = XmlParser.parse("<root><child>ChildValue</child><child>AnotherValue</child></root>");
String values = root.getValue(" ");
System.out.println(values); // Outputs: ChildValue AnotherValue

docs.title: Deleting by Path
docs.text:
The XmlNode class allows deleting nodes and their entire subtrees. You can do this by manually removing the children or by using the delete method. This method expects a path expression to identify the node to be deleted.

The path can be absolute or relative.

Example:

XmlNode root = XmlParser.parse("<root><child>Value</child></root>");
root.delete("/root/child");

System.out.println(root.xml());

Output: 

<root></root>

Info

1. If the specified path matches multiple nodes, all matching nodes are deleted.
2. Attempting to delete the root node is ignored to preserve the tree structure.

docs.title: Cloning Nodes
docs.text:
The cloning feature allows creating independent copies of nodes, including their attributes and child nodes. This ensures that modifications to the cloned node do not affect the original.

The clone() method creates a deep copy of the node:

XmlNode original = new XmlNode("original");
original.setValue("value");
XmlNode clone = original.clone();

System.out.println(clone.getName());  // Outputs: original
System.out.println(clone.getValue()); // Outputs: value

Info

1. The cloned node will not retain a parent reference to avoid circular dependencies.
2. All attributes and child nodes are also cloned.

docs.title: Namespace Binding
docs.text:
Although the class is not namespace-aware, the XmlNamespace feature allows binding namespaces to nodes.

Example:

XmlNode root = new XmlNode("root");
XmlNamespace ns = new XmlNamespace("ns", "http://example.com");
root.bind(ns);

System.out.println(root.xml());

Output: 

<root xmlns:ns="http://example.com"/>

It is worth noting that even the XmlNode class is not namespace-aware, you can create XML structure with multiple namespaces and prefixes by using the correct syntax in the XML string.

For example to create this XML structure:

<Document xmlns="urn:swift:xsd:xsys.012.001.01" xmlns:Sw="urn:swift:snl:ns.Sw" xmlns:SwInt="urn:swift:snl:ns.SwInt" xmlns:SwGbl="urn:swift:snl:ns.SwGbl">
    <xsys.012.001.01>
        <DlvryNtfctn>
            <Sw:SnFRef>NOTPROVIDED</Sw:SnFRef>
            <SwInt:RequestHeader>
                <SwInt:Requestor>AAAABEBBTG2</SwInt:Requestor>
                <SwInt:Responder>BBBBGB21XXX</SwInt:Responder>
            </SwInt:RequestHeader>
        </DlvryNtfctn>
    </xsys.012.001.01>
</Document>

You can use the following code:

    XmlNode root = new XmlNode("Document");

    // add al the namespaces declaration along the prefixes as normal attributes
    root.addAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("xmlns", "urn:swift:xsd:xsys.012.001.01"));
    root.addAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("xmlns:Sw", "urn:swift:snl:ns.Sw"));
    root.addAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("xmlns:SwInt", "urn:swift:snl:ns.SwInt"));
    root.addAttribute(new XmlNodeAttribute("xmlns:SwGbl", "urn:swift:snl:ns.SwGbl"));

    // then use the prefix as needed when creating the nodes
    XmlNode xsys = root.create("xsys.012.001.01");
    XmlNode DlvryNtfctn = xsys.create("DlvryNtfctn");
    DlvryNtfctn.create("Sw:SnFRef", "NOTPROVIDED");

The XmlNode class writer and parser will ignore the "xmlns" attribute meaning, and will also ignore the fact that some attributes and node elements contain a special character ":" in their name.

However, when this is injected as parameter for the MX xsys model parser for example, jaxb will take care of the namespaces and prefixes as expected.

docs.title: Removing Namespace Declarations
docs.text:
It is possible to remove all namespace declarations from an XML message by parsing the XML and converting it back to a string, omitting the namespace information in the process.

Example:

    ...
    assertTrue(xml.contains("<Saa:Priority>Normal</Saa:Priority>"));
    XmlNode xmlNode = XmlParser.parse(xml);
    String ns = xmlNode.xml();
    assertTrue(ns.contains("<Priority>Normal</Priority>"));

docs.title: Parsing Errors
docs.text:
Errors during parsing are logged, and null is returned for invalid XML:

XmlNode rootNode = XmlParser.parse("<invalid>");
if (rootNode == null) {
    System.out.println("Failed to parse XML.");
}

docs.title: Path Navigation Errors
docs.text:
Gracefully handle invalid paths:

try {
    XmlNode result = root.getNodeByPath("invalid/path");
    if (result == null) {
        System.out.println("Path not found.");
    }
} catch (Exception e) {
    System.err.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
}

docs.title: Node Creation Errors
docs.text:
When creating nodes dynamically using the create() method, any invalid paths or operations (e.g., using .. in paths) result in an IllegalArgumentException.

Example:

try {
    XmlNode root = new XmlNode("root");
    root.create("../invalid");
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getMessage()); // Outputs: Cannot apply the path segment .. to a root element
}

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
1. Avoid creating large node trees when memory is constrained.
  2. Use the removeEmptyElements() method to clean up unnecessary nodes in memory-intensive applications.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Input Validation: Ensure XML content is valid before parsing.
  2. Memory Management: Avoid creating excessively large node trees to prevent memory overflow.
  3. Error Logging: Check logs for detailed error information when parsing fails.
  4. Use Paths Effectively: Leverage path expressions and predicates to simplify navigation and filtering.
  5. Absolute paths: Use absolute paths for clarity when navigating or modifying nodes.
  6. Validation: Regularly validate XML content before processing to avoid unexpected parsing errors.
  7. Safe Node Manipulation: Combine the clone() and delete() methods to safely manipulate nodes without affecting the original tree structure.

docs.title: Prowide Integrator Translations - Overview
docs.text:
The Translations library provides out-of-the-box conversions between MT and ISO 20022 messages.

The library is used in runtime, as a regular dependency, to convert messages on the fly.

The conversion process is based on a set of rules that are embedded in the implementation and are maintained by Prowide as the standards change.

The translation is built on top of the Prowide Core and Prowide ISO 20022 message model. Therefore, the same API and classes used for parsing or building the messages are used as parameters and return values of the translation.

Automatic message conversion is also possible by means of a Factory that given a source message in either MT or MX format can autodetect the message type and find a suitable translator implementation for its equivalent in the other standard.

docs.title: Javadoc
docs.text:
Online javadoc

Prowide Integrator Translations Javadoc SRU2025-10.3.x

docs.title: Available Translations
docs.text:
The following table contains all out-of-the-box translations. The provided implementations within its internal mapping logic are based on the equivalence tables defined by SWIFT.

Notice there is no linear correlation between the source and target of the available translation, meaning that if A can be translated to B, the reverse is not always true.

The tables below are only a general reference. New translations are added on a regular basis. For a most accurate and up-to-date list, please check the actual classes available in the com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations package of your distribution, and in the restricted ISO 20022 version subpackages such as com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.cbpr and com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.sic.
