docs.title: FEDWIRE / CBPR+
docs.text:
For FEDWIRE in particular, back and forth translations are supported to convert the domestic US format to the international CBPR+ format and viceversa.

source target FEDWIRE pacs.008 CBPR+ pacs.008 CBPR+ pacs.008 FEDWIRE pacs.008 FEDWIRE pacs.009 CBPR+ pacs.009 COV CBPR+ pacs.009 COV FEDWIRE pacs.009

docs.title: Post-translation customization
docs.text: The translation library provides comprehensive mappings between MT and MX messages. However, there are scenarios where the default mapping behavior needs to be adjusted for specific business requirements.

docs.title: When to use post-translation customization
docs.text: Before implementing post-translation customization, consider the following alternatives:

docs.title: 1. Translator Configuration
docs.text:
The library provides a TranslatorConfiguration class with options to customize translation behavior without code changes. Review the available options for:

  • Address mapping (structured vs. lines)
  • Decimal places enforcement
  • Truncation evidence
  • Charset conversion
  • Coverage reporting

If your requirement can be addressed through configuration, prefer that approach.

docs.title: 2. Market-specific translators
docs.text:
The library provides specialized translator implementations for different markets and clearing systems (CBPR+, T2, RITS, SIC, LYNX, etc.). These implementations include market-specific mapping rules that may already address your needs.

Use the TranslatorFactoryProvider to obtain the appropriate translator for your target market:

GenericTranslatorFactory factory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getFactory(TranslatorStandard.CBPR);

docs.title: 3. Request mapping enhancements
docs.text: If you identify a mapping behavior that should be improved in the library itself (not a customer-specific requirement), contact Prowide support to request the enhancement. General improvements benefit all users and are incorporated into future library releases.

docs.title: 4. Post-translation customization
docs.text:
Post-translation customization should be considered exceptional and used only when:

  • The TranslatorConfiguration options do not address your requirement
  • The requirement is specific to your organization and not a general mapping improvement
  • Market-specific translators do not provide the needed behavior

This page describes how to customize the translated message after the standard translation has been applied.

docs.title: Post-processing approach
docs.text:
The recommended approach for customizing translation output is to post-process the translated message. This involves:

  1. Performing the standard translation using the library
  2. Modifying specific elements in the resulting message as needed

This approach has several advantages:

  • No library modifications required - Works with the standard library distribution
  • Full control - Complete flexibility to adjust any element in the translated message
  • Maintainability - Customizations are isolated in your code, making upgrades easier
  • Transparency - Clear separation between standard translation and business-specific adjustments

docs.title: Basic pattern
docs.text:
// 1. Translate using the standard library
GenericTranslatorFactory factory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getFactory(TranslatorStandard.CBPR);
Translator<AbstractMT, MxPacs00800108> translator = factory.getTranslator(mt103);
MxPacs00800108 mx = translator.translate(mt103);

// 2. Post-process to customize specific elements
customizeInstructionForNextAgent(mt103, mx);

// 3. Use the customized message
String xml = mx.message();

docs.title: Example: Field 72 to InstructionForNextAgent mapping
docs.text: A common customization need is adjusting how MT field 72 (Sender to Receiver Information) maps to the MX InstrForNxtAgt/InstrInf elements.

docs.title: Default behavior
docs.text:
The standard translation concatenates all field 72 lines and splits them by 35-character boundaries:

MT Field 72 input:
:72:/REC/BENEFICIARY REFERENCE
/INV/INVOICE-2024-00123
/ACC/MAIN

Default MX output (35-char split):
<InstrForNxtAgt>
    <InstrInf>/REC/BENEFICIARY REFERENCE/INV/INV</InstrInf>
</InstrForNxtAgt>
<InstrForNxtAgt>
    <InstrInf>OICE-2024-00123/ACC/MAIN</InstrInf>
</InstrForNxtAgt>

docs.title: Custom behavior: Line-by-line mapping
docs.text:
Some business requirements call for preserving the original line structure:

Customized MX output (line-by-line):
<InstrForNxtAgt>
    <InstrInf>/REC/BENEFICIARY REFERENCE</InstrInf>
</InstrForNxtAgt>
<InstrForNxtAgt>
    <InstrInf>/INV/INVOICE-2024-00123</InstrInf>
</InstrForNxtAgt>
<InstrForNxtAgt>
    <InstrInf>/ACC/MAIN</InstrInf>
</InstrForNxtAgt>

docs.title: Implementation options
docs.text: Two implementation approaches are available depending on whether the source MT message is accessible:

docs.title: Option 1: Using source MT (recommended)
docs.text:
When the source MT103 is available, extract the original field 72 lines directly:

public static void remapInstructionForNextAgent(MT103 mt103, MxPacs00800108 mx) {
    Field72 field72 = mt103.getField72();
    if (field72 == null) {
        return;
    }

    // Codes that have dedicated MX mappings (should be excluded)
    List<String> excludedCodes = Arrays.asList("ACC", "INS", "INTA", "SVCLVL", "LOCINS", "CATPURP");

    // Get original lines from field 72
    String value = field72.getValue();
    if (value == null) {
        return;
    }

    List<String> lines = Arrays.stream(value.split("\\r?\\n"))
            .filter(line -> !line.isEmpty())
            .collect(Collectors.toList());

    // Filter out codes that have dedicated MX mappings
    List<String> filteredLines = lines.stream()
            .filter(line -> excludedCodes.stream().noneMatch(code -> line.startsWith("/" + code + "/")))
            .collect(Collectors.toList());

    // Clear existing InstrForNxtAgt elements and repopulate
    var tx = mx.getFIToFICstmrCdtTrf().getCdtTrfTxInf();
    tx.getInstrForNxtAgt().clear();

    if (filteredLines.isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }

    // Repopulate with original lines (max 6 per CBPR+ schema)
    for (int i = 0; i < Math.min(filteredLines.size(), 6); i++) {
        InstructionForNextAgent11 instr = new InstructionForNextAgent11();
        instr.setInstrInf(filteredLines.get(i));
        tx.getInstrForNxtAgt().add(instr);
    }
}

docs.title: Option 2: Using MX content only
docs.text:
When the source MT is not available, reconstruct the lines by parsing the concatenated content:

public static void remapInstructionForNextAgent(MxPacs00800108 mx) {
    // Pattern to identify field 72 instruction codes: /CODE/
    Pattern codePattern = Pattern.compile("/[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{1,9}/");

    // Codes that have dedicated MX mappings
    List<String> excludedCodes = Arrays.asList("ACC", "INS", "INTA", "SVCLVL", "LOCINS", "CATPURP");

    var tx = mx.getFIToFICstmrCdtTrf().getCdtTrfTxInf();
    List<InstructionForNextAgent11> existing = tx.getInstrForNxtAgt();

    if (existing == null || existing.isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }

    // Concatenate all existing InstrInf values
    String concatenated = existing.stream()
            .map(InstructionForNextAgent11::getInstrInf)
            .filter(s -> s != null)
            .collect(Collectors.joining());

    if (concatenated.isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }

    // Parse by /CODE/ pattern to reconstruct original lines
    List<String> parsedLines = parseByCodePattern(concatenated, codePattern);

    // Filter excluded codes
    List<String> filteredLines = parsedLines.stream()
            .filter(line -> excludedCodes.stream().noneMatch(code -> line.startsWith("/" + code + "/")))
            .collect(Collectors.toList());

    // Clear and repopulate
    tx.getInstrForNxtAgt().clear();

    for (int i = 0; i < Math.min(filteredLines.size(), 6); i++) {
        InstructionForNextAgent11 instr = new InstructionForNextAgent11();
        instr.setInstrInf(filteredLines.get(i));
        tx.getInstrForNxtAgt().add(instr);
    }
}

private static List<String> parseByCodePattern(String content, Pattern pattern) {
    List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
    Matcher matcher = pattern.matcher(content);

    List<Integer> positions = new ArrayList<>();
    while (matcher.find()) {
        positions.add(matcher.start());
    }

    // Split at each /CODE/ position
    for (int i = 0; i < positions.size(); i++) {
        int start = positions.get(i);
        int end = (i + 1 < positions.size()) ? positions.get(i + 1) : content.length();
        String segment = content.substring(start, end);
        if (!segment.isEmpty()) {
            result.add(segment);
        }
    }

    // Handle case where no /CODE/ pattern found
    if (result.isEmpty() && !content.isEmpty()) {
        result.add(content);
    }

    return result;
}

MX-only approach limitation

The MX-only approach relies on heuristic pattern matching. It works well when field 72 lines follow the /CODE/value format, but may not handle all edge cases such as free-form text without codes. When possible, prefer the MT-based approach.

docs.title: Other customization scenarios
docs.text: The same post-processing pattern can be applied to customize other elements:

docs.title: Modifying party identifiers
docs.text:
// After translation
MxPacs00800108 mx = translator.translate(mt103);

// Customize debtor agent BIC
mx.getFIToFICstmrCdtTrf()
    .getCdtTrfTxInf()
    .getDbtrAgt()
    .getFinInstnId()
    .setBICFI("CUSTOMBICC");

docs.title: Adding optional elements
docs.text:
// After translation
MxPacs00800108 mx = translator.translate(mt103);

// Add regulatory reporting
RegulatoryReporting3 regRpt = new RegulatoryReporting3();
regRpt.setDbtCdtRptgInd(RegulatoryReportingType1Code.CRED);
// ... configure other fields
mx.getFIToFICstmrCdtTrf().getCdtTrfTxInf().getRgltryRptg().add(regRpt);

docs.title: Clearing specific elements
docs.text:
// After translation
MxPacs00800108 mx = translator.translate(mt103);

// Remove instruction for creditor agent if not needed
mx.getFIToFICstmrCdtTrf().getCdtTrfTxInf().getInstrForCdtrAgt().clear();

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Validate after customization - Always validate the modified message to ensure it remains schema-compliant
  2. Document customizations - Keep clear documentation of what modifications are applied and why
  3. Isolate customization logic - Create dedicated utility classes for customizations to keep code organized
  4. Consider upgrade impact - When upgrading the library, review if customizations are still needed
  5. Test thoroughly - Include test cases that verify both the standard translation and customizations

docs.title: FED ↔ CBPR+ Translations
docs.text:
The Prowide Integrator provides bidirectional translations between FED (Federal Reserve Fedwire) ISO 20022 messages and CBPR+ (Cross-Border Payments and Reporting Plus) messages.

These are MX to MX translators that convert between different ISO 20022 variants. Although they translate between MX formats (not MT to MX), they implement the same Translator interface as the MT/MX translators and provide a similar API for consistency.

These translators handle the conversion between:

  • FED: Domestic US payment system using routing numbers (9-digit ABA numbers)
  • CBPR+: SWIFT's restricted ISO 20022 subset for cross-border payments using BIC codes

docs.title: Supported Message Types
docs.text:
The following pacs message types are supported for bidirectional translation:

Message Type Description FED → CBPR+ CBPR+ → FED pacs.008 Customer Credit Transfer Fed_CbprMxPacs00800108_Translation CbprMxPacs00800108_Fed_Translation pacs.009.COV FI Credit Transfer (with customer layer) Fed_CbprMxPacs00900108COV_Translation CbprMxPacs00900108COV_Fed_Translation

docs.title: Key Translation Features
docs.text:
When translating from FED to CBPR+, the following transformations are applied:

  • Member ID to BIC mapping: FED routing numbers (9-digit) are mapped to BIC codes (8 or 11 characters)
  • AppHdr version conversion: FED uses AppHdr v3 (BusinessAppHdrV03), CBPR+ uses AppHdr v2 (BusinessAppHdrV02)
  • Settlement method conversion: FED CLRG (clearing) is converted to CBPR+ INDA (interbank settlement)
  • Business service: CBPR+ business service is set according to message type (swift.cbprplus.02 for pacs.008, swift.cbprplus.cov.02 for pacs.009.COV)
  • InstrId truncation: CBPR+ restricts InstrId to max 16 characters, while FED allows 35 characters. Truncation is tracked in the translator's truncation list.
  • BizPrcgDt removal: BusinessProcessingDate is removed from AppHdr (not supported in CBPR+ BAH v2)

When translating from CBPR+ to FED, the following transformations are applied:

  • BIC to Member ID mapping: BIC codes are mapped to FED routing numbers (9-digit ABA numbers)
  • AppHdr version conversion: CBPR+ AppHdr v2 is converted to FED AppHdr v3
  • Settlement method conversion: CBPR+ INDA is converted to FED CLRG
  • Message ID conversion: CBPR+ message IDs are converted to FED IMAD format (YYYYMMDD + 8-char ID + 6-digit sequence)
  • FedwireFunds envelope: Messages are wrapped in the FED FedwireFunds envelope with appropriate message type
  • Business service: FED business service is set from configuration (default: PROD)

docs.title: FED to CBPR+ Translation
docs.text:
Single customer credit transfer (pacs.008) example:

import com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx.cbpr.MxPacs00800108;
import com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.fedwire.*;

// Create translator
Fed_CbprMxPacs00800108_Translation translator = new Fed_CbprMxPacs00800108_Translation();

// Configure member ID to BIC mappings
FedToCbprTranslationConfiguration config = translator.getConfiguration();
config.addMemberIdToBicMapping("021000021", "CHASUS33XXX");  // JP Morgan Chase
config.addMemberIdToBicMapping("026009593", "BOFAUS3NXXX");  // Bank of America

// Translate FED XML to CBPR+
String fedXml = "..."; // FED pacs.008 XML
MxPacs00800108 cbprMsg = translator.translate(fedXml);

// Get CBPR+ XML output
String cbprXml = cbprMsg.message();

Cover payments include both the financial institution layer and the underlying customer credit transfer.

import com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx.cbpr.MxPacs00900108COV;
import com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.fedwire.*;

// Create translator
Fed_CbprMxPacs00900108COV_Translation translator = new Fed_CbprMxPacs00900108COV_Translation();

// Configure member ID to BIC mappings
FedToCbprTranslationConfiguration config = translator.getConfiguration();
config.addMemberIdToBicMapping("021000021", "CHASUS33XXX");

// Translate FED to CBPR+ cover
String fedXml = "..."; // FED pacs.009.COV XML
MxPacs00900108COV cbprMsg = translator.translate(fedXml);

Info

Notice the FED source payload is provided as a plain string containing the XML. While the CBPR+ target is returned as a parsed MxPacs00800108 or MxPacs00900108COV model object. You can get the XML string from the CBPR+ object using its message() method.

docs.title: CBPR+ to FED Translation
docs.text:
Single customer credit transfer (pacs.008) example:

import com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx.cbpr.MxPacs00800108;
import com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.fedwire.*;

// Create translator
CbprMxPacs00800108_Fed_Translation translator = new CbprMxPacs00800108_Fed_Translation();

// Configure BIC to member ID mappings
CbprToFedTranslationConfiguration config = translator.getConfiguration();
config.addBicToMemberIdMapping("CHASUS33XXX", "021000021");  // JP Morgan Chase
config.addBicToMemberIdMapping("BOFAUS3NXXX", "026009593");  // Bank of America

// Set business service (optional, default is "PROD")
config.setBusinessService("PROD");

// Parse CBPR+ message
String cbprXml = "..."; // CBPR+ pacs.008 XML
MxPacs00800108 cbprMsg = MxPacs00800108.parse(cbprXml);

// Translate CBPR+ to FED
String fedXml = translator.translate(cbprMsg);

// FED XML is now ready for Fedwire submission
System.out.println(fedXml);
Cover payments include both the financial institution layer and the underlying customer credit transfer.

import com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx.cbpr.MxPacs00900108COV;
import com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.fedwire.*;

// Create translator
CbprMxPacs00900108COV_Fed_Translation translator = new CbprMxPacs00900108COV_Fed_Translation();

// Configure BIC to member ID mappings
CbprToFedTranslationConfiguration config = translator.getConfiguration();
config.addBicToMemberIdMapping("CHASUS33XXX", "021000021");
config.addBicToMemberIdMapping("BOFAUS3NXXX", "026009593");

// Parse CBPR+ message
String cbprXml = "..."; // CBPR+ pacs.009.COV XML
MxPacs00900108COV cbprMsg = MxPacs00900108COV.parse(cbprXml);

// Translate CBPR+ to FED
String fedXml = translator.translate(cbprMsg);

// FED XML is now ready for Fedwire submission
System.out.println(fedXml);

Info

Notice the CBPR+ source payload is provided as a parsed MxPacs00800108 or MxPacs00900108COV model object. If you have the plain XML as source content you can parse it into the corresponding cbpr model object. While the FED target is returned as a plain string containing the XML.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
As observed in the examples above, both translators provide configuration options to manage the routing number ↔ BIC mappings and other settings.

Configuration for FED → CBPR+ translations:

Fed_CbprMxPacs00800108_Translation translator = new Fed_CbprMxPacs00800108_Translation();
FedToCbprTranslationConfiguration config = translator.getConfiguration();

// Add individual member ID to BIC mapping
config.addMemberIdToBicMapping("021000021", "CHASUS33XXX");

// Load mappings from a map
Map<String, String> mappings = new HashMap<>();
mappings.put("021000021", "CHASUS33XXX");
mappings.put("026009593", "BOFAUS3NXXX");
config.loadMemberIdMappingsFromStrings(mappings);

// Clear all mappings
config.clearMemberIdMappings();

// Get all mappings
Map<String, BIC> allMappings = config.getMemberIdToBicMap();

Key methods:

  • addMemberIdToBicMapping(String memberId, String bicCode): Add a mapping from FED member ID to BIC
  • mapMemberIdToBic(String memberId): Get the BIC for a member ID (returns null if not found)
  • loadMemberIdMappingsFromStrings(Map<String, String> mappings): Bulk load mappings
  • clearMemberIdMappings(): Clear all mappings

For CBPR+ → FED translations similar routing number ↔ BIC mapping configuration is provided. And also the ability to set the FED business service (default: "PROD"):

CbprMxPacs00800108_Fed_Translation translator = new CbprMxPacs00800108_Fed_Translation();
CbprToFedTranslationConfiguration config = translator.getConfiguration();

// Set business service (default: "PROD")
config.setBusinessService("TEST");

// Add individual BIC to member ID mapping
config.addBicToMemberIdMapping("CHASUS33XXX", "021000021");

// Load mappings from a map
Map<String, String> mappings = new HashMap<>();
mappings.put("CHASUS33XXX", "021000021");
mappings.put("BOFAUS3NXXX", "026009593");
config.loadBicMappingsFromStrings(mappings);

// Clear all mappings
config.clearBicMappings();

// Get all mappings
Map<BIC, String> allMappings = config.getBicToMemberIdMap();

docs.title: Precondition Checks
docs.text:
Preconditions are validations performed on the source message before translation to ensure it meets the necessary criteria for a successful conversion. These are only implemented for FED ↔ CBPR+ translators, checking:

  • Message type check: Validates that the FED message has the expected message type (pacs.008 or pacs.009) by checking the AppHdr/MsgDefIdr element
  • pacs.009.COV specific: Validates that the FED pacs.009 message contains the UndrlygCstmrCdtTrf element (required for cover payments)

docs.title: Message ID Conversion (CBPR+ → FED)
docs.text:
The CBPR+ to FED translator generates IMAD-compliant message IDs:

  • Format: YYYYMMDD (8 digits) + source ID (8 chars, alphanumeric) + sequence (6 digits)
  • Example: 202501091234ABCD000001
  • Sequence counter is independent per translator class (pacs.008 vs pacs.009)
  • The source ID is created from the first 8 alphanumeric characters of the CBPR+ AppHdr/MsgId
  • If the source ID has fewer than 8 alphanumeric characters, it is right-padded with zeros
  • If the source ID has more than 8 alphanumeric characters, it is truncated to the first 8
  • The sequence is a zero-padded 6-digit number starting at 000001 and incrementing with each translation performed by the same translator instance

Translator Instance Reuse

The translator classes are stateful and re-entrant. You should create only one instance of each translator and reuse it for multiple translations. The CBPR+ to FED translators use a static sequence generator for IMAD message IDs that is tied to the translator class instance. Creating multiple instances will reset the sequence counter, potentially generating duplicate message IDs.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
1. Routing Number ↔ BIC Mapping: You must provide mappings between FED routing numbers and BIC codes. The translators do not include built-in mappings.

  2. Currency Restriction: FED messages are restricted to USD currency only, while CBPR+ supports multiple currencies.

  3. Single Transaction: Both FED and CBPR+ restrict to exactly one CdtTrfTxInf per message (unlike general ISO 20022 which allows multiple).

  4. AppHdr Version: FED uses AppHdr v3, CBPR+ uses AppHdr v2. The translators handle this conversion automatically.

  5. Settlement Method: FED typically uses CLRG (clearing), while CBPR+ uses INDA (interbank settlement). The translators convert this automatically.

  6. Message Validation: For production use, consider running additional CBPR+ or FED schema validation on the translated output.

docs.title: Translation classes
docs.text:
Translations are normally one to one, from a source message into a target message.

Each available translation implementation, given a source message type and a target message type, is implemented in a specific class. The message types are explicit in the class names and also in the class parameters for the translation call.

For example:

Class name Source message type Target message type MT103_STP_MxPacs00800102_Translation MT 103 STP pacs.008.001.02 MxPacs00900102_MT202COV_Translation pacs.009.001.02 MT 202 COV

In the most simple use case scenario the translation is called like this:

MT103 mt = MT103.parse(fin);
try {
    MT103_MxPacs00800108_Translation t = new MT103_MxPacs00800108_Translation();
    MxPacs00800108 mx = t.translate(mt);
} catch(final LogicalMessageCriteriaException e1) {
    System.out.println("logical message criteria exception: "+e1.getMessage());
} catch(final TranslationPreconditionException e2) {
    System.out.println("precondition exception: "+e2.getMessage());
}
In the code above, we create an instance of the specific translation, and we call the translate method passing the source message as parameter. The result is the target message.

And the revers from MX to an MT analogously.

Notice translation classes are not thread safe, so a new instance must be created for each translation.

The precondition and logical criteria checks are explained in the following sections, but that is basically a way to check if the source message is suitable for the specific translation, and if the target message will be valid after the translation.

docs.title: Logical message criteria
docs.text:
The logical message criteria is a condition evaluated on the source message, to know if it is selectable for the specific translation.

In most cases, there is only a single available equivalence for the translation. This is mostly the case when converting from MX to MT. However, in some cases, a single message can be translated to more than one target option. This is due to the fact that in the MT standard, there are many message types that can be used for different functions. While in the MX standard, there are specific message types for each function.

For example, an MT502 could be a Redemption Order or a Subscription Order, meaning the same MT structure can be used for two different functions. While its MX equivalences have two specific message types for the Redemption and Subscription, setr.004.002.01 or setr.010.002.01.

This criteria evaluation is checked automatically when the translation is run. It can be switched off by configuration, and optionally called by the application before the translation.

docs.title: Manual criteria check
docs.text:
All translation classes have a translatable method that is used to check the logical criteria. This method checks the content of the source message and returns true or false if it is suitable for the specific translation.

MT545 for example could be translated to a sese.025, sese.020, sese.026 or sese.035. Since in the MX standard, there are specific types for each use case, while in the MT all functions are covered by the same message type 545.

If you call the translatable method for all possible translations using the same MT source for example:

MT545 mt = MT545.parse(fin);
MT545_MxSese02500109_Translation t1 = new MT545_MxSese02500109_Translation();
MT545_MxSemt02000201_Translation t2 = new MT545_MxSemt02000201_Translation();
MT545_MxSese02600201_Translation t3 = new MT545_MxSese02600201_Translation();
MT545_MxSese03500201_Translation t4 = new MT545_MxSese03500201_Translation();
t1.translatable(mt, true));
t2.translatable(mt, true));
t3.translatable(mt, true));
t4.translatable(mt, true));
Then, for a given valid MT, only one of the options should return true while the others should return false.

You can do the above manually, in a sequence of IF/ELSE conditions. Or you can just use the translator factory. The translator factory does exactly that, it checks given a source message what output is translatable.

Although, notice there are a few situations where the same input could be translated seamlessly to more than one output. In such cases the translator factory returns a default.

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
Each specific translation may implement its own preconditions. This is a condition evaluated on the source message, to make sure the created target message will be valid. It is mainly used when the target message has some mandatory content that is optional in the source message.

These preconditions are checked automatically when the translation is run. They can be switched off by configuration, and optionally called by the application before the translation.

docs.title: Manual precondition check
docs.text:
Preconditions on the source message can be checked explicitly before attempting the translation, or can be caught from an exception calling the translation method in a try block.

The following method will check all the message preconditions and will return a list of precondition errors.

    final MT564_MxSeev03900202_Translation translator = new MT564_MxSeev03900202_Translation();
    final MT564 source = MT564.parse(sample);

    try {
        // The precondition being check is:
        // IF ((B2[*]\97a Account\SAFE\97C\Account Code ContainsString 'GENR') And ((B2[*]\95a Party\ACOW IsPresent) Or ((B2[*]\94a Place\SAFE IsPresent) Or (B2[*]\93a Balance IsPresent))))
        // this pseudo-code is available in the translator javadoc
        List<PreconditionError> p = translator.preconditionsCheck(source);

        if (p.isEmpty()) {
            // Call the translation process
            final MxSeev03900202 mx = translator.translate(source);

            // Print content from the translated message
            System.out.println("Cancellation Reason Code: " + mx.getCorpActnCxlAdvc().getCxlAdvcGnlInf().getCxlRsnCd().name());
            System.out.println("Processing Completness: " + mx.getCorpActnCxlAdvc().getCxlAdvcGnlInf().getPrcgSts().getEvtSts().getEvtCmpltnsSts().name());
            System.out.println("Corporate Action Id: " + mx.getCorpActnCxlAdvc().getCorpActnGnlInf().getCorpActnEvtId());
            System.out.println("Event Type Code: " + mx.getCorpActnCxlAdvc().getCorpActnGnlInf().getEvtTp().getCd().name());
            System.out.println("Underlying Security ISIN: " + mx.getCorpActnCxlAdvc().getCorpActnGnlInf().getUndrlygSctyId().getISIN());

        } else {
            // Print precondition errors
            for (PreconditionError e : p) {
                System.out.println("precondition error: " + e.getCode() + " " + e.getDescription());
            }
        }

    } catch (final LogicalMessageCriteriaException e1) {
        System.out.println("logical message criteria exception: " + e1.getMessage());
    }

In the above example the translator is any instance of a Translator implementation. When the translation is from MT to MX the expected parameter is the MT. When the translation is from MX to MT the expected parameter is the MX.

If the returned list is empty, the source message satisfies all preconditions. If not, each element in the list will contain a code and a description of the condition that is not satisfied.

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
In order for the target message to be valid, these premises should be satisfied:

  • The source message should be valid. Notice the translation module will not run full compliance message validation, neither on source nor target messages. However, the Prowide Integrator Validation module can be used for this purpose.

  • The logical message criteria check should pass: meaning the source message should be selectable for the specific translation applied.

  • The preconditions on the source message should pass.

Regardless of this contract, since the translation is sensitive to the data, if the translated message is going to be sent through the network it is recommended that as the last step of the process the validation is run on the created message.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Regardless of the specific translation mappings, the target message header is always filled with data from the source or with derived content as follows:

Translation Source element Target element MT to MX Block 1 SenderBlock 2 ReceiverFixed from target message identifierCurrent date and timeMain message referenceTrailer PDE AppHdr FromAppHdr ToAppHdr Message DefinitionAppHdr Creation Date and TimeAppHdr Business Message IdentifierAppHdr Possible Duplicate Emission(By default the ISO Business Header is created, not the legacy Application Header) MX to MT AppHdr From *AppHdr To *AppHdr Possible Duplicate EmissionFixed from target message identifier(both ISO Business Header and legacy Application Header are supported) Block 1 SenderBlock 2 ReceiverTrailer PDEBlock 2 message type(Direction is Input by default. The rest of the MT headers data is filled with proper defaults)

* If the AppHdr is not present, the translation attempts to use the parties BIC codes in the Group Header element within the MX Document. If none is found, then the MT is populated with default BIC codes. Also, both BIC and DN structures are supported, when the DN is used the BIC is extracted and filled with the default branch code.

This default mapping can be overridden by configuration. In the TranslationConfiguration class that can be optionally passed to the translator call, a fixed specific sender and/or receiver can be set. The configuration will take precedence on any other default or mapped value. For example:

    MT103 mt = translator.translate(mx, new TranslationConfiguration().setSender(new BIC("ABCDARXX")));

docs.title: Message direction
docs.text:
In MT messages, the direction is explicit in the message structure because the headers are mandatory and there is one specific header for outgoing messages and another specific header for incoming messages. So when you have an MT payload, you know the direction.

This is not true for MX, where the direction is not in the payload (AppHdr + Document), but in the transmission wrapper, and that is dependent on the specific interface.

When the message is converted from MX to MT, there is no longer an explicit direction, so by default all translators from MX to MT will generate an input message. An Input message means the message is going to be sent to SWIFT.

If in the MX to MT translation process, in your host application, you know the generated MTs should be Output because you have received the original MX from SWIFT then you can use a configuration to switch the direction. This is done passing the optional TranslationConfiguration to the translation call. For example:

    MT103 mt = translator.translate(mx, new TranslationConfiguration().setDirection(MessageDirection.Output));

The MT content will be the same, but in the headers the sender and receiver will be reconfigured as Output (received) message.

docs.title: Truncation
docs.text:
When the source element value does not fit in the target message field, the translation will truncate the content. This could happen specially when translating from MX to MT, where the MT fields are shorter than the MX elements.

By default, the truncation is done with evidence, meaning in the translated messages the truncated content will contain an explicit '+' symbol at the end of the field. This is done to indicate that the content has been truncated.

Along that, the translation class stores the original and truncated content so that a report can be generated with the truncated elements. This report can be generated by calling the getTruncatedContent() method in the translator.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
For MX to MT translations, a coverage report can be generated by calling the getCoverageReport() method in the translator. This report will show the elements of the source MX elements that have been mapped into the target MT.

Notice in most situations the coverage report will not be 100% because there are many elements in the source MX that cannot be mapped into the target MT. The idea of the coverage report is to analyse if for certain use cases the key elements in the MX have been mapped.

docs.title: M to N translations
docs.text: Although translation implementations are always one to one, there are some use cases where a single MX message can contain data corresponding to multiple MT messages. In other words, where a business operation, report, or transaction in an MX message cannot be mapped into a single MT because of the limitations of the MT standard.

docs.title: setr.015 to MT515
docs.text:
The switch order confirmation in an MX setr.015 can contain multiple switch operations, and for each it can contain multiple redemption and subscription legs. Thus, the translation to achieve should receive a single setr.015 and convert that into multiple MT515 messages.

To keep the translation API simple and consistent, in these situations more than one translation implementation is made available for the given source and target message types. IN the swift order confirmation example, this is achieved by two translators:

Class name Source message type Target message type MxSetr01500104_MT515_Redemption_Translation setr.015.001.04 MT 515 MxSetr01500104_MT515_Subscription_Translation setr.015.001.04 MT 515

Where the first translation implementation will convert the redemption leg data from the MX into an MT515 with the instrument sell, and the second translator will convert the subscription leg data from the MX into another MT515 with the instrument buy.

The host application or the process running the translation is expected to use both translators, passing as parameters the same source MX message. The first call will create the redemption, while the second call, with the same source MX parameter, will create the subscription.

docs.title: pain.001 to MT101
docs.text:
The payment initiation in a pain.001 can contain multiple payment information elements, each having multiple credit transfers. The default 1 to 1 translation implemented in the MxPain00100103_MT101_Translation class will use as source content only the first payment information element. Each credit transfer in this source element will be mapped into a repetitive sequence B in the target MT. But a single MT will be created.

A special 1 to many implementations for this use case is provided in the MxPain00100103_MT101_BulkTranslation class. The translation methods in this class return a List<MT101> instead of a single instance. This implementation uses internally the one to one mapping, but will process all the available payment information elements in the source MX. For each payment information in the MX a single MT101 is created. As for the credit transfer repetitions within each payment information element, multiple sequences B are created in the corresponding MT101 instance.

The 1 to 1 translation implemented in the MxPain00100103_MT101_Translation can be considered a special case of the MxPain00100103_MT101_BulkTranslation where the result will be a list with a single element.

The drawback of the special bulk translation is that it cannot implement the generic translator API, thus it will not be recognized by the Translators Factory.

docs.title: camt.053 to MT940
docs.text:
The camt.053 can contain multiple account statements, each with multiple entries.

The implementation actually iterates over the Statement elements in the source pacs message, applying for each a similar mapping to the 1 to 1 translation MxCamt05300102_MT940_Translation.

A special 1 to many implementation for this use case is provided in the MxCamt05300102_MT940_BulkTranslation class. The translation methods in this class return a List<MT940> instead of a single instance. This implementation uses internally the one to one mapping, but will process all the available account statements in the source MX. For each statement in the MX a single MT940 is created. As for the transaction entries within each statement, multiple sequences 61 are created in the corresponding MT940 instance.

docs.title: Generic translations
docs.text: Generic translation calls, without knowing in advance the source message type, can be done in two ways. Using the Translator interface or using the TranslatorFactory. This is particularly useful when translating and inbound queue of receiving a variety of unknown message types.

docs.title: Translator interface
docs.text:
All MT and MX translation classes implement the common translation interface Translator. This interface is helpful in situations where generic translation must be implemented, consolidating the translation of several message types in a single processing unit.

The following method uses this interface to translate any MT receiving the translation implementation and specific source message as parameters:

    private static AbstractMX doTranslation(final Translator translator,final AbstractMT msg){
        AbstractMX mx=null;
        try{
            mx = translator.translate(msg);
        } catch(final LogicalMessageCriteriaException e1) {
            System.out.println("logical message criteria exception: "+e1.getMessage());
        } catch(final TranslationPreconditionException e2) {
            System.out.println("precondition exception: "+e2.getMessage());
        }
        return mx;
    }
Notice any MT or MX can be parsed into a generic model without knowing the specific message type. In the example below the fin variable contains the plain MT content in a String.

    AbstractMT mt = AbstractMT.parse(fin);

The reverse from MX to MT can be seamlessly achieve. There is a parse available in the AbstractMX class that can be used to parse any MX message content into a generic model. And the Translator interface can be used to translate the generic model into a specific MT message.

    AbstractMX mx = AbstractMX.parse(xml);

docs.title: Translator factory
docs.text:
To automatically obtain a suitable translator instance, a TranslatorFactory is available. The factory takes an MT or MX message as a parameter and returns the appropriate translator for that message.

    Translator t = TranslatorFactory.getTranslator(msg);

The above method, for example, when an MT103 is passed, would return an instance of the MT103_MxPacs00800110_Translation translation implementation. And when the parameter is an MxPacs00800110 message the returned translator will be MxPacs00800110_MT103_Translation. Meaning the same factory is used to either MT to MX or MX to MT translations.

Notice the MX version may be different from the example, depending on the latest version available.

So the whole block of code to run any generic translation would be like this:

    AbstractMX mx = AbstractMX.parse(xml);
    Translator t = TranslatorFactory.getTranslator(mx);
    if (t != null) {
        try {
            AbstractMT mt = t.translate(mx);
        } catch() {
            (...)
        }
    }

And conversely for MT to MX:

    AbstractMT mt = AbstractMT.parse(fin);
    Translator t = TranslatorFactory.getTranslator(mt);
    if (t != null) {
        try {
            AbstractMX mx = t.translate(mt);
        } catch() {
            (...)
        }
    }

The getTranslator method can also accept a TranslatorFactoryConfiguration as an argument. In the following example, a TranslatorFactoryConfiguration for IAP v1.2 is obtained and customized for a specific clearing system:

    AbstractMT mt = AbstractMT.parse(fin);

    TranslatorFactoryConfiguration tfc = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getConfiguration(TranslatorStandard.IAP_v1_2);
    tfc.setClearingSystem(CashClearingSystemCode.NBO);

    Translator t = TranslatorFactory.getTranslator(mt, tfc);

    if (t != null) {
        try {
            AbstractMX mx = t.translate(mt);
        } catch() {
            (...)
        }
    }

For a detailed explanation of TranslatorFactoryConfiguration, Please see the Translator Provider factory and the Translator Factory Configuration sections.

The null check is important because the factory might not find a suitable translator for the given message. This could happen when the message type is not supported or when the message content does not meet the logical criteria or preconditions for the translation.

When converting from MT to MX several translator implementations might be available, to create different versions of the same output MX message type. In this situation, by default, the factory will return the translator for the latest version available.

docs.title: Factory selection criteria
docs.text:
Internally the factory applies different methods in cascade to narrow the available options and to finally select the specific translator instance to return:

  1. Existing translation implementation for the specific source message type
  2. Logical message criteria applied to the source message type
  3. Optional, preconditions check applied to the source message type
  4. Optional, preferred specific target message type

In any of the steps above if the options are reduced to a single candidate, that translator is returned. Otherwise, the factory returns null.

The main logic to pickup one translation over another one is by applying the logical message criteria on the source message. These criteria are implemented when the equivalence is not 1 to 1. Most of the available translations are a 1 to one equivalence, but in some exceptional cases, you might have in particular some MT that can be used for multiple functions while in the MX standard there are specific types for each use case.

This logic is implemented in each translator classe and is used by the factory to determine which translator instance to create.

As a result, the getTranslator call for an MT502 could return either MT502_MxSetr01000201_Translation, MT502_MxSetr00400201_Translation or null depending on the function of the MT message. And by function we refer to the source message content. Thus, the criteria check involves inspecting the source message content.

The javadoc for the translator implementations describes the specific criteria for each translator.

Complete example: https://github.com/prowide/prowide-integrator-examples/blob/master/src/main/java/com/prowidesoftware/swift/samples/integrator/translations/MtMxTranslationExample3.java

docs.title: Factory preconditions check
docs.text:
Besides the logical message criteria, the factory can also check the preconditions (when available for the translator). This check is skipped by default because despite the logical message criteria, a source message could be translated even if it does not meet the preconditions.

The host application can always retrieve the translator from the factory, and then check the preconditions itself to handle any errors. When this is not the preferred option, the factory can be configured to use also the precondition check for the translator selection like this:

    translatorFactory.getTranslator(msg, 
        new TranslatorFactoryConfiguration().setEvaluatePreconditions(true));

While this reduces logic in the calling application, the drawback is that the factory might return null when there is no selectable translator instance and the application will not know if the issue comes from a failed logical message criteria or by a failed precondition.

The precondition check main goal is to ensure that the translated message will be valid.

docs.title: Disambiguation and preferred equivalences
docs.text:
For certain translations, there might be multiple target message types available, because there is no internal content criteria to determine the target message type.

In these cases, the factory will return a proper default. However, the factory can be configured to use a preferred equivalence based on pattern expressions.

The parameter is available in the TranslatorFactoryConfiguration class and can be used like this:

    TranslatorFactory.getTranslator(new MT103(), 
            new TranslatorFactoryConfiguration()
                        .withTranslationMappings(Collections.singletonList("MT103:pacs.008.001.08"));

In this example, when translating from an MT103 message, the factory will pick up the 08 version of the MX instead of using the latest available version as default.

Or:

    TranslatorFactory.getTranslator(new MxPacs00900108(),
                new TranslatorFactoryConfiguration()
                        .withTranslationMappings(Collections.singletonList("pacs.009.001.08:MT200.*"));

In this other example, when translating from a pacs.009.001.08 the factory will pick up the MT200 as target message type instead of the default MT202.

Each entry in this List is a String that defines a mapping from a source message type to one or more target message types. The general format is:

"SOURCE : TARGET1, TARGET2,...,TARGETN".

Example:

MT103: pacs.008.001.02, pacs.008.002.08: This mapping indicates that the source message type MT103 is primarily translated to pacs.008.001.02. If this target is not available, the system attempts to translate to pacs.008.002.08, and if this too is unavailable, it will resort to any other available target.

Flexibility with Wildcards:

Wildcards ( * ) are particularly useful in specifying a range of message types. For instance, using * with an MtId or MXid allows the system to select any message type within the specified range, prioritizing the most recent version available. Examples include camt.* to match any camt message, pacs.008.001.* to match any version of pacs.008.001, and pain.*.*.03 to match any pain message with the version 03 regardless of its business process or functionality.

It is important to notice that the target message type must be a valid equivalence and with a translation implementation available in the library, otherwise the factory will return null.

This way of customizing the factory might be useful for instance in situations where the expected output message type is received as parameter from the user or exported service. On the contrary, it does not make much sense to use this parameter hard-coded in the application, since in that case where the versions are fixed and known, it is better to create the specific translator instance directly.

Notice the above makes more sense in the MT to MX, where more than one option for tha target message may be available. In the MX to MT case, the situation is simpler since normally there is a single target MT type for any given MX.

docs.title: Custom Translator Factory
docs.text:
For some use cases the list of required translations and versions is very strict. Thus, it might be convenient to create your own translator factory instead of parameterizing the library defaults. This allows you to dynamically choose the right translation implementation for a given message.

In essence, a translator factory is basically any class that receives a source message and returns a Translator instance. So there are no restrictions on how to implement it.

However, here's an example of how to create a simple translator factory leveraging the translatable method of the translator to apply the logical criteria and preconditions check:

    public Translator getTranslator(AbstractMX source, boolean checkPreconditions) {
        final String identifier = source.getMxId().id();
        switch (identifier) {
            case "pacs.004.001.09": {
                MxPacs00400109Ch02_MT103_Translation t = new MxPacs00400109Ch02_MT103_Translation();
                if (t.translatable((MxPacs00400109Ch02) source, checkPreconditions)) {
                    return t;
                }
                break;
            }
            case "pacs.008.001.08": {
                MxPacs00800108Ch02_MT103_Translation t = new MxPacs00800108Ch02_MT103_Translation();
                if (t.translatable((MxPacs00800108Ch02) source, checkPreconditions)) {
                    return t;
                }
                break;
            }
            case "pacs.009.001.08": {
                MxPacs00900108Ch03 mx = (MxPacs00900108Ch03) source;
                MxPacs00900108Ch03_MT202COV_Translation tCOV = new MxPacs00900108Ch03_MT202COV_Translation();
                if (tCOV.translatable(mx, checkPreconditions)) {
                    return tCOV;
                }
                MxPacs00900108Ch03_MT202_Translation t = new MxPacs00900108Ch03_MT202_Translation();
                if (t.translatable(mx, checkPreconditions)) {
                    return t;
                }
                break;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

In this example, the CustomTranslatorFactory class defines a getTranslator method that takes the source MX message and a boolean flag to indicate whether preconditions should be checked. Inside the method, you can use a switch statement or any logic you prefer to select the appropriate translation class based on the message identifier (identifier). The translatable method is called for each potential translation class to check if it's suitable for the given source message.

In situations such as dealing with pacs.009 messages, where there may be multiple target options, you may want to test each of them to determine the appropriate translation.

Additionally, there are cases where multiple target options are available, and the logical criteria check does not provide a clear choice. In such cases, you'll need to make a decision based on your specific requirements.

Creating a custom translator factory allows you to dynamically select the most suitable translator class for a given source message, enhancing the adaptability of your translation process.

docs.title: Using the Custom Translator Factory
docs.text:
To use the custom translator factory, you can call its getTranslator method when you need to perform a translation:

CustomTranslatorFactory factory = new CustomTranslatorFactory();
AbstractMX sourceMessage = // Initialize your source MX message here

boolean checkPreconditions = true; // Set to true if you want to check preconditions

Translator translator = factory.getTranslator(sourceMessage, checkPreconditions);

if (translator != null) {
    // Perform the translation using the selected translator
    // ...
} else {
    // Handle the case when no suitable translator is found
    // ...
}

This approach gives you the flexibility to dynamically choose the appropriate translation class based on the source message type, making your translation process more adaptable to different scenarios.

docs.title: Market Type translations
docs.text:
Depending on the user group, central bank RGTS, clearing system, or market infrastructure; specific translations might be required.

The Prowide translations module is implemented in layers. We have a set of base mappings that are common to all clearings or market types translators. The base mappings are defined in the TranslatorStandard enum.

Standard Description ISO ISO 20022 CBPR+ Cross Border Payments IAP Iso Accelerator Pack (v1.1 and v1.2) SWIFTGO SWIFT GPI

This standard translators can be used as is, or also as a base implementation to derive more specific translators, in particular, for the different clearing systems such as: SIC, RITS, CHATS, SCRIPS, MEPS, T2S, LYNX, FISC, EBA, etc...

docs.title: Translator Provider factory
docs.text:
To facilitate access to these specific translations, a TranslatorFactoryProvider class is available.

This class receives either a clearing system code or just a standard and returns the specific factory for it.

  • For the clearing system codes, the CashClearingSystemCode enum is used. This enumeration contains all the clearing system codes defined in the ISO 20022 external code set.
    GenericTranslatorFactory translatorFactory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getTranslatorFactory(CashClearingSystemCode.BOF);
  • For the standard translators, the TranslatorStandard enum is used. This enumeration contains all base standard mappings available in the library, such as CBPR+.
    GenericTranslatorFactory translatorFactory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getTranslatorFactory(TranslatorStandard.CBPR);

Then, the returned GenericTranslatorFactory interface provides the necessary API to inject a specific message instance and get the corresponding translator for it.

    GenericTranslatorFactory translatorFactory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getTranslatorFactory(CashClearingSystemCode.MEP);

    AbstractMT mt = AbstractMT.parse(fin);
    Translator t = translatorFactory.getTranslator(mt);
    if (t != null) {
        AbstractMX mx = t.translate(mt);
    }

In the code above, the factory automatically detects the message type, determines the applicable equivalence, and returns the corresponding translator. Depending on the message payload, the factory could return null if the message is not supported or cannot be translated for the requested clearing or standard type.

docs.title: Translator packages.
docs.text:
Depending on the specific clearing system, the translations are implemented in different packages. Thus, instead of the translator class implementation being located in the com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations package, it could get classes in more specific packages such as com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.cbpr or com.prowidesoftware.swift.translations.sic.

This distribution in packages is implementation dependent and is not exposed to the user. Anyway, all translator classes implement the Translator interface and can be used in the same way.

Specific packages and thus specific translators are available for the following clearing systems:

Clearing System Description SIC Swiss RGTS RITS Australian RGTS CHATS Hong Kong RGTS SCRIPS Legacy Singapore Clearing and Payment System MEPS MEPS+ Singapore RGTS T2S TARGET2 LYNX Canadian RGTS FISC Taiwan RGTS EBA EURO E1-S1 clearing

Tip

All non-listed clearing systems are supported and are based by default on IAP v1.2. Meaning if you request
a translator for a clearing system not listed above, the factory will return the IAP v1.2 translator but
with the clearing code set to the requested clearing system. These clearing systems could be for example:
ABE, ART, AVP, AZM, BAP, BCC, BGC, BHS, BIC, BKA, BNB, BOC, BOL, BPI, BPS, BRB, BRC, BRI, BRL, BRM, BRS, BRT, 
BRZ, BSB, BSC, BSI, BSL, BSM, BSP, BSS, etc...

docs.title: Model classes
docs.text:
Two special considerations are required when using these translation factories for the specific market types CBPR and SIC. And in particular for the MX to MT translations.

The AbstractMX object expected for the CBPR+ and SIC translator is not a standard message model from the com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx package, but a model from the specific packages com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx.cbpr and com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx.sic respectively.

So you can use the same factory provider procedure as above, but the AbstractMX object should be the result of parsing the XML with specific model classes.

In order to do this on a generic way, without knowing the specific model class, you can use the message factories for both restricted ISO models:

    GenericTranslatorFactory translatorFactory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getTranslatorFactory(TranslatorStandard.CBPR);

    AbstractMX mx = CbprMessageFactory.createMessage(fin);
    Translator t = translatorFactory.getTranslator(mx);
    if (t != null) {
        AbstractMT mt = t.translate(mx);
    }

And analogously for the SIC messages:

    GenericTranslatorFactory translatorFactory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getTranslatorFactory(CashClearingSystemCode.SIC);

    AbstractMX mx = SicMessageFactory.createMessage(fin);
    Translator t = translatorFactory.getTranslator(mx);
    if (t != null) {
        AbstractMT mt = t.translate(mx);
    }

For the rest of translations, the standard com.prowidesoftware.swift.model.mx package is used in all translator parameters, both in the MX to MT and MT to MX translations.

docs.title: Clearing code mapping
docs.text:
When the translator for a specific clearing is requested via the TranslatorFactoryProvider, the factory will already know the clearing code to apply in the message header.

Although, if the source MT contains a clearing code in field 103 of the block 3 header, this code will be propagated into the MX group header settlement information.

For example this MT header:

{1:F01BANKUS33AXXX0001000001}{2:O2020805240820FOOONO22AXXX13908885502408200706N}{3:{103:NBO}"

Will generate the following content in the MX group header:

<SttlmInf>
    <SttlmMtd>CLRG</SttlmMtd>
    <ClrSys>
        <Cd>NBO</Cd>
    </ClrSys>
</SttlmInf>

And the reverse translation will also map the clearing system code back to the MT block 3 field 103.

This clearing codes in the header are handy when implementing for example an MT to MX service to handle translation for many clearing systems. In this case, the following logic could be used to select a proper translations factory depending on the clearing code in the MT header:

    AbstractMT mt = AbstractMT.parse("...");

    // extract clearing code from MT header
    String clearingCode = null;
    SwiftBlock3 b3 = mt.getSwiftMessage().getBlock3();
    if (b3 != null) {
        clearingCode = b3.getTagValue(Field103.NAME);
    }

    GenericTranslatorFactory factory;

    if (clearingCode == null) {
        // if there is no clearing code, use the CBPR+ factory (just as an example)
        factory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getFactory(TranslatorStandard.CBPR);

    } else if (EnumUtils.isValidEnum(CashClearingSystemCode.class, clearingCode)) {
        factory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getFactory(CashClearingSystemCode.valueOf(clearingCode));

    } else {
        // if the clearing code is not valid, use the ISO 20022 factory that will propagate the clearing code as is
        factory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getFactory(TranslatorStandard.ISO_20022);
    }

    // create the actual translator
    Translator<AbstractMT, AbstractMX> translator = factory.getTranslator(mt);

    if (translator != null) {
        // translate the message
        AbstractMX mx = translator.translate(mt);
        System.out.println(mx.message());
    }

The above example will generate an MX with the expected CLRG and ClrSys elements in the group header. And if the MT does not have any clearing code, it will generate the CBPR+ message with INDA as settlement method and no clearing system code.

docs.title: Translator factory configuration
docs.text:
When the mechanism implemented by the TranslatorFactoryProvider is not enough, and specific configurations are required, the TranslatorFactoryConfiguration object can be used.

With this configuration object you can customize a GenericTranslatorFactory to meet specific needs.

The getConfiguration method from the GenericTranslatorFactory interface returns this object and you can use the available methods to set the desired configuration.

In the example below, a CBPR+ based factory is created. Then a specific AppHdr version and a business service are defined:

    GenericTranslatorFactory translatorFactory = TranslatorFactoryProvider.getTranslatorFactory(TranslatorStandard.CBPR);

    TranslatorFactoryConfiguration tfc = translatorFactory.getConfiguration();
    tfc.setAppHdrType(AppHdrType.BAH_V4);
    tfc.addBusinessServiceMapping("*", "swift.foobar.test.01");
    tfc.addBusinessServiceMapping("pacs.008.001.08", "swift.foobar.test.02");

    AbstractMT mt = AbstractMT.parse(fin);
    Translator t = translatorFactory.getTranslator(mt);
    if (t != null) {
        AbstractMX mx = t.translate(mt);
    }

With this configuration, all translated messages will generate the version 4 of the AppHdr and a BizSvc with the value "swift.foobar.test.01", except for pacs.008.001.08, which will use "swift.foobar.test.02".

Additional configuration can be defined in the TranslatorFactoryConfiguration, see also Factory preconditions check and Disambiguation and preferred equivalences.

docs.title: MT to MX
docs.text: Translation from MT messages to its MX equivalent is done using the specific classes name MTnnn_Mxmmm_Translation, where nnn corresponds to a specific translatable MT and mmm to its available MX representation.

docs.title: Class selection
docs.text:
The first step to perform a message translation is to select the proper translation to use. The specific translation class depends mainly on the message type, but in several cases also on the message content.

MT103 for example, has two flavors (STP and not STP) for the source message, while the target MX is the same for both, so the available translation are:

  • MT103_STP_MxPacs00800102_Translation
  • MT103_MxPacs00800102_Translation

A different example can be seen for MT564, where the same message type can be translated to several Mx messages depending on the message functionality (deductible from content):

  • MT564_MxSeev03100202_Translation
  • MT564_MxSeev03500202_Translation
  • MT564_MxSeev03900202_Translation
  • MT564_MxSeev04400202_Translation

While the selection of a proper translation combination to apply is a responsibility of the calling application, the correctness of the call is checked at several points:

  • First by the translation classes. You cannot invoke an MT103_MxPacs00800102_Translation passing and MT202 as parameters. Also, you cannot assign the result of that translation to an invalid Mx.
  • Second, by the message logical criteria checks. These checks are performed internally by the translation process, and a runtime LogicalMessageCriteriaException is thrown if the criteria is not satisfied. For example in the MT564 example, these criteria checks are mainly based on the function of the corporate action message, defined in field 23G, so that a "cancellation" won't be translated into a "confirmation".
  • Third, by the message preconditions. When all the above is correct, numerous content preconditions are checked to ensure that the source message can be effectively translated to the target message.

docs.title: Translation call
docs.text:
The translation procedure is invoked with the translation method of the specific translation class. The following example shows how to translate an MT 564 into its corresponding MX seev.039.002.02:

The MT is parsed into an MT564 object using any of the providing parsing methods:

    final MT564 source = MT564.parse(sample);

A proper instance of translation is created:

    MT564_MxSeev03900202_Translation translator = new MT564_MxSeev03900202_Translation();

And finally, the translation method is invoked in a try to catch the logical message criteria and preconditions exceptions.

    try {
        final MxSeev03900202 mx = (MxSeev03900202) translator.translate(source);
    } catch (final LogicalMessageCriteriaException e1) {
        System.out.println("logical message criteria exception: " + e1.getMessage());
    } catch (final TranslationPreconditionException e2) {
        System.out.println("precondition exception: " + e2.getMessage());
    }

If the MT564 satisfies all preconditions, the mx variable will contain the resulting MX message. Then all the MX API can be used to retrieve content from the converted message, or it can be serialized to its XML representation.

  System.out.println("Cancellation Reason Code:" +
  mx.getCorpActnCxlAdvc().getCxlAdvcGnlInf().getCxlRsnCd().name());
  System.out.println(mx.message());4

docs.title: Business Header
docs.text:
Depending on the source MT, some fields might be mapped to the target MX business header, which is optional.

To check the created header in XML: In the created MX object, the message() or document() calls will serialize just the Document portion of the MX, while header() will serialize the header if it is present. Alternatively, you can call message(String, boolean) which will generate both header (if present) and document in a single XML under the indicated wrapper element.

To check header in Java model: The getBusinessHeader() will return the model representation with the header.

Complete example: https://github.com/prowide/prowide-integrator-examples/blob/master/src/main/java/com/prowidesoftware/swift/samples/integrator/translations/MtMxTranslationExample1.java

docs.title: Translator Configuration
docs.text:
The TranslatorConfiguration class provides optional settings to customize the translation behavior. Access the configuration via getConfiguration() on the translator instance.

MT103_MxPacs00800108_Translation translator = new MT103_MxPacs00800108_Translation();
translator.getConfiguration().setUseStructuredAddressesIfPossible(true);
MxPacs00800108 mx = translator.translate(mt103);

MX to MT
docs.text: Translation from MX messages to its MT equivalent is done using the specific classes name Mxmmm_MTnnn_Translation, where mmmm corresponds to a specific translatable MX and nn to its available MT representation.

docs.title: Class selection
docs.text:
The first step to perform a message translation is to select the proper translation to use. The specific translation class depends mainly on the message type, but in several cases also on the message content.

MxPacs00800102 for example can only be translated into an MT103. However, MxPacs00900102 can be used to create MT202 in both flavors; STP and not STP, so the available translation are:

  • MxPacs00800102_MT103_Translation
  • MxPacs00900102_MT202_Translation
  • MxPacs00900102_MT202COV_Translation

In the above example, a different set of preconditions apply to create the MT202 for STP or not.

A different example can be seen for MxSeev03100202, where the same message type can be translated to several target MT messages:

  • MxSeev03100202_MT564_Translation
  • MxSeev03100202_MT568_Translation

While the selection of a proper translation combination to apply is a responsibility of the calling application, the correctness of the call is checked at several points:

  • First by the translation classes. You cannot invoke an MxSeev03100202_MT564_Translation passing anything different from a MxSeev03100202 as source message parameter. Also, you cannot assign the result of that translation to an invalid MT.
  • Second, by the message logical criteria checks. These checks are performed internally by the translation process, and a runtime LogicalMessageCriteriaException is thrown if the criteria is not satisfied.
  • Third, by the message preconditions. When all the above is correct, many content preconditions are checked to ensure that the source message can be effectively translated to the target message.

docs.title: Translation call
docs.text:
The translation procedure is invoked with the translation method of the specific translation class. The following example shows how to translate a MxSeev03400202 into its corresponding MT 567:

The source message can be created using the MX API or parsing its content from an XML file or string.

    MxSeev03400202 mx = new MxSeev03400202();
    mx.setBusinessHeader(new BusinessHeader(new BusinessApplicationHeaderV01()));
    mx.getBusinessHeader().getBusinessApplicationHeader().setBizMsgIdr("MYID");
    mx.setCorpActnInstrStsAdvc(new CorporateActionInstructionStatusAdviceV02Subset());
    mx.getCorpActnInstrStsAdvc().setCorpActnGnlInf(new CorporateActionGeneralInformation13());
    mx.getCorpActnInstrStsAdvc().getCorpActnGnlInf().setCorpActnEvtId("777");

A proper instance of translation is created:

    MxSeev03400202_MT567_Translation translator = new MxSeev03400202_MT567_Translation();
And finally, the translation method is invoked in a try to catch the logical message criteria and preconditions exceptions.

    try {
        final MT567 mt = (MT567) translator.translate(mx);
    } catch (final LogicalMessageCriteriaException e1) {
        System.out.println("logical message criteria exception: " + e1.getMessage());
    } catch (final TranslationPreconditionException e2) {
        System.out.println("precondition exception: " + e2.getMessage());
    }

If the MX satisfies all preconditions, the mt variable will contain the resulting MT message. Then all the MT API can be used to retrieve content from the converted message, or it can be serialized to its SWIFT FIN representation.

    System.out.println(mt.message());

Complete example: https://github.com/prowide/prowide-integrator-examples/blob/master/src/main/java/com/prowidesoftware/swift/samples/integrator/translations/MxMtTranslationExample1.java

docs.title: Translator Configuration
docs.text:
The TranslatorConfiguration class provides optional settings to customize the translation behavior. Access the configuration via getConfiguration() on the translator instance.

MxPacs00800102_MT103_Translation translator = new MxPacs00800102_MT103_Translation();
translator.getConfiguration().setTruncateWithEvidence(false);
MT103 mt = translator.translate(mx);

docs.title: Precondition and criteria checks
Truncation
docs.text:
Option Default Description setTruncateWithEvidence(boolean) true When true, adds a '+' symbol at the end of truncated content (when allowed by the target charset).

See Truncation details below for more information.

docs.text:
Option Default Description setMxToMtCharsetConversionEnabled(boolean) true Replaces characters not supported in FIN (charset x) with a dot. Also sanitizes XML escape sequences. setPreserveWhitespaces(boolean) false When true, preserves leading and trailing whitespaces from source XML elements.

See Sanitize below for more information.

Option Default Description setEnableCoverageReport(boolean) true Tracks which MX elements were read during translation. Can be disabled for performance.

See Coverage report below for more information.

docs.title: Message identifiers
docs.text: Option Default Description setSender(BIC) null Overrides the sender BIC in the created MT message. Also applies to MT→MX. setReceiver(BIC) null Overrides the receiver BIC in the created MT message. Also applies to MT→MX. setDirection(MessageDirection) Input Sets the message direction. Use Output to create an MT with Output block 2. setGeneratePossibleDuplicateFlag(boolean) true Maps the possible duplicate flag from MX header to MT trailer. Also applies to MT→MX. setUseSystemCreationDateTime(boolean) false When true, uses current system date/time instead of AppHdr CreationDate.
